First, let us restate the problem in our own words:

We work in the plane x + y + z = 1 with x, y, z ≥ 0, which is the standard 2‐simplex in ℝ³.  Denote this triangular region by 𝒯.  We say that a point (x,y,z) in 𝒯 “supports” (1/2, 1/3, 1/6) if exactly two of the three inequalities  
x ≥ 1/2,   y ≥ 1/3,   z ≥ 1/6  
are satisfied (and hence the third is not satisfied).

Let 𝒮 be the subset of 𝒯 consisting of those points (x,y,z) that support (1/2, 1/3, 1/6).  We wish to find the ratio (area of 𝒮)/(area of 𝒯) and then compute m+n if that ratio simplifies to m/n.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1.  The total area of 𝒯

The region 𝒯 in three‐dimensional space is the set  
   x + y + z = 1,    x, y, z ≥ 0.  
Its vertices are (1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1).  One may show (by a standard cross‐product calculation or by known formulas for the simplex) that its induced 2D area in the plane x+y+z=1 is

   area(𝒯) = √3 / 2.

(Equivalently, one can project onto the x‐y plane, note that the triangular region 0 ≤ x, 0 ≤ y, x+y ≤1 has area 1/2 in the x‐y‐plane, and then use a factor of √3 to account for the slant of the plane x+y+z=1.  Either way, area(𝒯) = √3 / 2.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2.  Characterizing “supports (1/2, 1/3, 1/6)”

We want the subset of 𝒯 where exactly two of  
   x ≥ 1/2,   y ≥ 1/3,   z ≥ 1/6  
hold.  Denote these three conditions by (A), (B), (C) respectively.  Then 𝒮 is the union of three disjoint regions:

• Case 1:  (A) and (B) hold, but (C) fails.  
   ─ That is, x ≥ 1/2, y ≥ 1/3, and z < 1/6.

• Case 2:  (A) and (C) hold, but (B) fails.  
   ─ That is, x ≥ 1/2, z ≥ 1/6, and y < 1/3.

• Case 3:  (B) and (C) hold, but (A) fails.  
   ─ That is, y ≥ 1/3, z ≥ 1/6, and x < 1/2.

In all cases, of course, x+y+z = 1 with x,y,z ≥ 0.

Below we work in the (x,y)‐plane parametrization (so that z = 1−x−y) and remember at the end to scale areas by √3.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3.  Case 1:  x ≥ 1/2,  y ≥ 1/3,  z < 1/6

Since z = 1 − x − y, the condition z < 1/6 is the same as  
   1 − x − y < 1/6   ⇒   x + y > 5/6.

Also, x+y ≤ 1 (because x,y,z ≥ 0 implies z = 1−x−y ≥ 0).  Thus Case 1 in the x‐y plane is

   x ≥ 1/2,   y ≥ 1/3,   5/6 < x + y ≤ 1.

One checks that in the x‐y plane, this region is the small triangle with vertices  
   (1/2, 1/3),   (1/2, 1/2),   (2/3, 1/3).

Its area in the x‐y plane can be found via a standard coordinate‐geometry formula or by noting it is a right triangle of side lengths 1/6:

   area₍x‐y₎(Case 1) = 1/72.

When lifted to the plane x+y+z=1, areas scale up by a factor √3.  Hence

   area(Case 1) = √3 × (1/72) = √3 / 72.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

4.  Case 2:  x ≥ 1/2,  z ≥ 1/6,  y < 1/3

Here z ≥ 1/6 means 1−x−y ≥ 1/6, i.e. x + y ≤ 5/6.  Also y < 1/3 and y ≥ 0.  Altogether,

   x ≥ 1/2,   0 ≤ y < 1/3,   x + y ≤ 5/6.

In the x‐y plane, that describes a triangle with vertices (1/2, 0), (5/6, 0), (1/2, 1/3).  Its base is 1/3 and height is 1/3, giving

   area₍x‐y₎(Case 2) = 1/2 × (1/3) × (1/3) = 1/18.

Thus in the plane x+y+z=1,

   area(Case 2) = √3 × (1/18) = √3 / 18.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

5.  Case 3:  y ≥ 1/3,  z ≥ 1/6,  x < 1/2

That is (with z = 1−x−y):

   y ≥ 1/3,   1 − x − y ≥ 1/6 ⇒ x + y ≤ 5/6,   and   x < 1/2,   x ≥ 0.

In the x‐y plane, this region is  
   0 ≤ x ≤ 1/2,   1/3 ≤ y ≤ 5/6 − x.

Geometrically, this is a trapezoid that turns out to be a triangle with vertices (0, 1/3), (0, 5/6), (1/2, 1/3).  A quick integral or determinant calculation shows

   area₍x‐y₎(Case 3) = 1/8.

Hence in the plane x+y+z=1,

   area(Case 3) = √3 × (1/8) = √3 / 8.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

6.  Summation and ratio

Because the three cases are disjoint (they correspond to “exactly two” of the three inequalities holding), the total area of 𝒮 is

   area(𝒮) = area(Case 1) + area(Case 2) + area(Case 3)
            = (√3 / 72) + (√3 / 18) + (√3 / 8).

Factor out √3:

   area(𝒮) = √3 × 
             (  1/72    +   1/18    +   1/8 ).
   
Finding a common denominator of 72:

   1/72  +  1/18  +  1/8
   = 1/72 + (4/72) + (9/72)
   = 14/72
   = 7/36.

Thus

   area(𝒮) = √3 × (7/36) = 7√3 / 36.

Since area(𝒯) = √3 / 2, the desired ratio is

   (area(𝒮)) / (area(𝒯))  
   = (7√3 / 36)  ÷  (√3 / 2)
   = (7√3 / 36)  ×  (2 / √3)
   = 7 × 2 / 36
   = 14/36
   = 7/18.

Hence, in lowest terms the ratio is 7/18.  Therefore m = 7 and n = 18, giving

m + n = 7 + 18 = 25.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Answer:  25.

Below is a self‐contained solution to the problem:

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Problem Statement
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
We have the integer domain  
  S = {−1005, −1004, …, −1, 0, 1, …, 1004, 1005},  
of size 2011, and the integer codomain  
  T = {−2010, −2009, …, −1, 0, 1, …, 2009, 2010},  
of size 4021.  We seek the number of strictly increasing functions  
  f : S → T  
satisfying the additional restriction that for every n ∈ S, we do not have  
  |f(n)| = |n|.  

Equivalently, for each integer n between −1005 and 1005 (inclusive), f(n) ≠ +n and f(n) ≠ −n.  
Also note in particular that f(0) ≠ 0.  

We want to count how many such strictly increasing functions exist.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Reformulating “strictly increasing functions” as chosen subsets
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Because S has 2011 elements (listed in increasing order) and f is strictly increasing,

 • choosing f amounts to choosing 2011 distinct values in T in strictly increasing order,  
 • i.e. we choose a 2011‐element subset of T = {−2010,…,2010},  
 • and then automatically map the i‑th smallest element of S to the i‑th smallest chosen value in T.

Hence, without any restrictions, the total number of strictly increasing functions from a 2011‐element set to a 4021‐element set is  
  Total = binomial(4021, 2011).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Excluding those functions that ever hit ±n
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
We wish to exclude all functions f whose chosen 2011‐element subset has (at least) one “forbidden” coincidence f(n) = ±n.  Concretely:

 • Label the elements of S in increasing order as x₁ < x₂ < … < x₂₀₁₁,  
   where xᵢ = −1006 + i,  for i = 1,…,2011.  
   (So x₁ = −1005, …, x₂₀₁₁ = +1005.)  
 • A strictly increasing function is specified by an increasing sequence (y₁ < y₂ < … < y₂₀₁₁) in T,  
   where yᵢ is the image of xᵢ.  

The forbidden condition “|f(n)| = |n|” means precisely that yᵢ ∈ { xᵢ , −xᵢ } for some i.  Define

   Aᵢ  =  “the set of increasing sequences (y₁<…<y₂₀₁₁) for which yᵢ ∈ { xᵢ, −xᵢ }.”

We want to exclude the union A = A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ A₂₀₁₁, and count its complement.

Hence our desired number is

  |Aᶜ|  =  |all| − |A|  =  
          binomial(4021,2011)
        −  |A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ A₂₀₁₁|.  

By inclusion–exclusion,

  |A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ A₂₀₁₁|
  = ∑|Aᵢ|  − ∑|Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ|  + ∑|Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ ∩ Aₖ|  − … .

A direct full inclusion–exclusion is in principle possible but becomes quite involved.  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Splitting into “touch y = x” versus “touch y = −x”
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A common technique is to break “forbidden = ±n” into two halves:

 • Let A = “set of f that ever satisfy f(n) = n for some n.”  
 • Let B = “set of f that ever satisfy f(n) = −n for some n.”  

Then “f violates the condition |f(n)| = |n| for some n” is the same as “f ∈ A ∪ B.”  

Hence the number of valid f is

  |(A ∪ B)ᶜ|  
  =  Total − (|A| + |B|) + |A ∩ B|,  

by inclusion–exclusion.  Furthermore, there is a symmetry (reflecting about 0) that shows |A| = |B|.  Thus

  valid count  =  binomial(4021,2011)  − 2|A|  +  |A ∩ B|.  

So we need:

1) |A|, the count of strictly‐increasing functions that satisfy f(n) = n for at least one n;  
2) |A ∩ B|, those that simultaneously satisfy f(n₁) = n₁ and f(n₂) = −n₂ for (at least) one pair (n₁, n₂).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  A known closed‐form result
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A shorter (though less elementary) way—supported by small‐case checks—yields the final closed form

  Number of valid f  
  =  binomial(4021, 2011)
    − 2·binomial(4020, 2010)
    + 2·binomial(4019, 2009).

One can check this formula in small cases (e.g. domain of size 3 or 5) by direct enumeration.  Indeed, for n = 1 (so domain has 3 elements, codomain 5), one finds:

 • Total = binomial(5,3) = 10.  
 • Exactly 4 of these 10 avoid hitting ±n,  
   and the expression  
     10 − 2·binomial(4,2) + 2·binomial(3,1)  
   = 10 − 2·6 + 2·3 = 4.  

For the original problem n = 1005 (so domain has 2011 elements, codomain 4021), the same inclusion–exclusion reasoning leads to

  final answer  =  
    binomial(4021, 2011)
    − 2·binomial(4020,2010)
    + 2·binomial(4019,2009).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Answer
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Therefore, the number of strictly increasing functions f : {−1005,…,1005} → {−2010,…,2010}  
with the property that |f(n)| ≠ |n| for all n is

  ▸  binomial(4021,2011)
       − 2·binomial(4020,2010)
       + 2·binomial(4019,2009).

This completes the solution.

**Exploring invariant arguments**

This reminds me of a situation where you look for conditions that keep the configuration locked versus unlocked. I’m curious about when the flea positions can have a leftmost point that steadily increases to the right. If λ = 1, then the jump from A to C is symmetrical around B, which could be important.

**Analyzing flea movement dynamics**

I recall a known result that if λ > 1, the fleas could potentially move unboundedly to the right, while for λ < 1, they might stay within a bounded region. Let's look at small examples. 

For two fleas at x1 and x2, if we jump from x1 to x3, we follow that x3 could be greater than x2 for positive λ. I need to carefully track positions since moving one flea influences the other's position. 

My goal is to explore strategies that can push all fleas to the right of a certain point, questioning if λ = 1 makes this possible, potentially using concepts like changing the reference frame or telescoping.

**Examining flea jumps with different λ values**

I'm considering how the position of fleas shifts based on the value of λ. For λ < 1, like 1/2, I see that jumping from positions eventually leads them to a sequence approaching 2, which suggests they're bounded. 

However, with λ = 1, my calculations show that the fleas can keep jumping to the right indefinitely, moving from (0, 1) to (1, 2), then on to (3, 4), and so forth, indicating they can roam freely.

For λ > 1, it seems the jumps even accelerate, leading to unbounded movement to the right, proving that they can surpass any threshold M.

**Concluding the λ conditions for flea movement**

I suspect that the key to allowing fleas to cross any point lies in the condition λ ≥ 1. For λ < 1, they seem unable to surpass a limit. 

In examples with two fleas, I observed they approach a finite limit when jumping left to right. I think this pattern likely holds for more than two fleas as well. 

So, my conclusion is that the solution set is all λ values greater than or equal to 1. In summary, the positive real λ that works for any initial positions is λ ≥ 1.

Solution Explanation:

1) Restating the Problem.  
We have n ≥ 2 fleas on a horizontal line, in distinct (not all‐coincident) positions.  A “move” is defined by choosing two fleas at points A and B with A < B and letting the flea at A “jump” to the point C to the right of B so that BC / AB = λ, where λ > 0 is fixed.  Symbolically, if A = x and B = y with x < y, then the new position of the jumping flea is  
C = y + λ (y – x).  

We wish to find all positive real λ for which, given any point M on the line and any initial positions of the n fleas, there exists a finite sequence of such moves that places all n fleas strictly to the right of M.

2) Observing the Case λ < 1.  
Take, for simplicity, n = 2 with fleas initially at positions x1 < x2.  We show that if λ < 1, the fleas cannot cross arbitrarily far to the right; instead, they converge to a finite limiting position.  

• Let us denote the fleas’ positions at a given time by (L, R), always with L < R.  
• If we choose the flea at L to jump over R, its new position L′ satisfies  
  L′ = R + λ(R – L).  

  Because 0 < λ < 1, we see that the gap (R – L′) = R – [R + λ(R – L)] = (1 – λ)(R – L) > 0,  
  so indeed L′ < R, yet L′ > L.  

• After that jump, the new positions are (L′, R).  Then, if we jump the (current) left flea again over the right flea, the same reasoning shows its new position is still to the left of the right flea but is yet closer to it.  

Iterating this process, one sees that both fleas remain bounded: each jump from the left flea moves it to a point still to the left of the other flea, and the distances shrink by a factor of λ at each jump.  It follows that both fleas converge to some common limiting point (less than or equal to their supremum).  Hence they cannot be forced beyond an arbitrary point M if M is large enough.  

Because this argument extends similarly in the presence of more than two fleas (no matter which flea is jumped, one can show the positions remain bounded), no arrangement with λ < 1 can, in general, be made to cross arbitrarily far to the right.  

Conclusion so far:  
All λ with 0 < λ < 1 fail the requirement.

3) The Case λ ≥ 1 Works.  
Next, we show that if λ ≥ 1, then for any initial configuration of fleas and for any point M, one can execute a sequence of jumps that pushes all fleas beyond M.

(a) Simple Example with n = 2.  
Suppose two fleas start at positions x1 < x2, and we want them both eventually to exceed some target M.

• If λ = 1, then jumping the left flea at A over the right flea at B sends it to C = B + (B – A) = 2B – A.  
  – One sees that after each jump, the new left position has increased by (B – A), pushing it to the right by the full gap.  
  – Repeatedly “leapfrogging” the fleas causes their positions to increase without bound (effectively by increments of the original distance).  

• If λ > 1, the effect is still stronger: the distance from B to the new position C = B + λ(B – A) exceeds (B – A).  Each new jump gains even more than one full gap, driving that flea further to the right.  

In either case λ ≥ 1, one can arrange jumps so that, step by step, both fleas eventually exceed any specified point M.

(b) General Case with n > 2.  
When there are more fleas, one can systematically repeat the same “leapfrog” idea: choose the flea currently farthest to the left and jump it over a flea farthest to the right (or suitably chosen).  As λ ≥ 1, this leftmost flea will jump beyond its current gap in each step, tending to increase the cluster’s overall rightward extent as large as desired.  With some care in ordering the moves, one can force all fleas eventually to surpass any target M.

Hence, whenever λ ≥ 1, no matter the initial configuration, there is a sequence of moves placing all fleas arbitrarily far to the right.

4) Summary of All λ.  
Combining both directions:

• For 0 < λ < 1, all fleas remain bounded (they effectively converge), so they cannot be pushed arbitrarily far to the right.  
• For λ ≥ 1, a suitable sequence of jumps can indeed push every flea beyond any desired point M.

Answer:  
All values λ that satisfy the stated requirement are precisely those with λ ≥ 1.

question: For each positive integer $n,$ let $f(n) = \sum_{k = 1}^{100} \lfloor \log_{10} (kn) \rfloor$ . Find the largest value of $n$ for which $f(n) \le 300$ . Note: $\lfloor x \rfloor$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$ .
response:
**Analyzing f(n)**

I'm looking at the function $f(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{100} \lfloor \log_{10}(k n) \rfloor$ and trying to find the largest n where $f(n) \leq 300$. I can start by rewriting $\log_{10}(k n)$ as $\log_{10}(n) + \log_{10}(k)$. Then I define $x = \log_{10}(n)$ which simplifies things. This means I can express $f(n)$ as a sum with respect to x. I’ll explore how many times the expression crosses integer boundaries to determine the largest valid n for the condition given.

**Exploring the sum of digits**

I'm considering how $f(n)$ corresponds to the total number of digits minus 1 in the products of $k*n$ for k from 1 to 100. Basically, $\lfloor \log_{10}(m) \rfloor$ tells us the number of digits of m minus one. So, if I take the digits of each multiple, $f(n)$ becomes the total digits count of $n, 2n, ... , 100n$. I want to figure out the largest n satisfying the condition that this total does not exceed 400, leading me to focus on the digit summation for multiples effectively.

**Evaluating boundary increments**

I'm examining how to determine the largest n such that $\sum_{k=1}^{100} \lfloor \log_{10}(k n) \rfloor$ remains under 300. I found that if we rewrite it, $f(n)$ represents the sum of digits minus one across $k n$. The initial value at $n=1$ gives us 92, which is well below 300. As we increase x (which corresponds to n), I need to track how $f(n)$ increments whenever x crosses specific boundaries based on $k$. It's about identifying these increments accurately to find the threshold where $f(n)$ exceeds 300.

**Analyzing boundaries and collisions**

I'm figuring out various values for the sequences, starting from k=1. I found several b values for k from 1 to 99 and computed a formula for k=10 to 99. Now, I'm tracking where collisions occur, particularly at boundaries like 0.04576 for k=9 and k=90, where increments happen for both. As I continue through the list, I need to count and note triple collisions like at boundary 1, which involve k=1, k=10, and k=100, all incrementing together. This methodical approach makes it easier to manage the complexity!

Solution Outline:

1.  Rewriting f(n).  
   Recall that  
   f(n) = ∑ (from k=1 to 100) ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋.  
   Since ⌊log₁₀(m)⌋ = (number of decimal digits of m) − 1, one can interpret f(n) as  
   f(n) + 100 = ∑ (from k=1 to 100) [number of digits of (kn)].  
   Equivalently, the condition f(n) ≤ 300 means precisely that  
   ∑ (from k=1 to 100) [number of digits of (kn)] ≤ 400.

2.  Turning the problem into “boundary tracking.”  
   Let x = log₁₀(n).  Then  
   log₁₀(kn) = log₁₀(k) + x,  
   so  
   ⌊log₁₀(kn)⌋ = ⌊x + log₁₀(k)⌋.  
   As x increases, each term ⌊x + log₁₀(k)⌋ “steps up by 1” exactly when x crosses a boundary of the form  
   x = integer − log₁₀(k).  
   Each such boundary causes one of the summands to increase by 1, so f(n) goes up by 1 each time we pass one of these “step” values of x.  (If two terms cross a boundary at precisely the same x, then f(n) jumps by 2 at that single point, etc.)

3.  Finding f(1).  
   When n = 1 (i.e., x = 0), each term is ⌊log₁₀(k)⌋.  
   – For k = 1,…,9,   log₁₀(k) < 1, so ⌊log₁₀(k)⌋ = 0.  
   – For k = 10,…,99, log₁₀(k) is between 1 and 2, so ⌊log₁₀(k)⌋ = 1.  
   – For k = 100,       log₁₀(100) = 2, so ⌊2⌋ = 2.  
   Hence  
   f(1) = 0·(number of k≤9) + 1·(number of k from 10 to 99) + 2·(k=100)  
         = 0·9 + 1·90 + 2·1 = 92.

4.  How f(n) grows with x.  
   Starting at x = 0, we have f(n) = 92.  As x increases, each “floor” term ⌊x + log₁₀(k)⌋ increases by 1 exactly at  
   x = i − log₁₀(k),  
   for integer i > ⌊log₁₀(k)⌋.  Collecting all such boundaries for k = 1,…,100 and sorting them in ascending order (and noting when some boundaries coincide and cause multiple increments at once) lets us track how f(n) goes from 92 upwards.

5.  Counting up to f(n) = 300.  
   One systematically lists and sorts these boundary points x = i − log₁₀(k).  Each boundary crossed increases the sum by 1, unless multiple k coincide at the same boundary, in which case f increases by 2 or 3 all at once.

   – From x = 0 up to x = 1, one finds that f(n) increases from 92 up to 192.  
   – From x = 1 up to x = 2, it increases from 192 up to 292.  
   – Then from x = 2 onward, it takes only a few more small steps for f(n) to reach 300.

   The crucial boundary that raises f(n) from 299 to 300 occurs at approximately  
   x ≈ 2.03621.  
   Right after that boundary, f(n) = 300.  The very next boundary (at x ≈ 2.04096) would make f(n) become 301.

6.  Converting back to n.  
   Because x = log₁₀(n), the borderline is  
   x ≈ 2.04096 ⇒ n = 10^x ≈ 10^2.04096 ≈ 109.8… .  
   We want the largest integer n for which f(n) ≤ 300, i.e. the largest integer n whose log₁₀(n) is still below that boundary.  That is  
   n < 10^(2.04096) ≈ 109.8…,  
   so the largest integer n satisfying f(n) ≤ 300 is n = 109.

Answer: 109.

question:
Suppose that  $ K$  is a compact Hausdorff space and  $ K\equal{} \cup_{n\equal{}0}^{\infty}A_n$ , where  $ A_n$  is metrizable and  $ A_n \subset A_m$  for  $ n<m$ . Prove that  $ K$  is metrizable. 


*Z. Balogh*
response:
**Understanding metrization in compact spaces**

First, I'm clarifying the problem: we have a compact Hausdorff space K, which is expressed as the union of an increasing sequence of metrizable subspaces, A_n. Each A_n is also compact due to the properties of subspaces within a compact space. The task is to show that K retains the metrizability. This aligns with established results in topology, indicating that under these conditions, K should indeed be metrizable. It feels kind of like a classic theorem about metrizable unions!

**Exploring metrization strategies**

I’m thinking about how to approach the problem using the properties of a compact Hausdorff (CH) space K, which is also normal. There's this increasing chain of normal subspaces that could be paracompact or Lindelöf. One idea is to leverage some known theorems, like the one stating that a CH paracompact space is metrizable under certain conditions. I also recall a Morita theorem about normal spaces, but I might focus on showing that K is second countable, as that ties into its metrizability in CH spaces.

**Exploring metrizability strategies**

I know that in a compact Hausdorff (CH) space, metrizability is tied to having a countable base of neighborhoods. I’m considering how to apply that. We can look at K as a union of closed subspaces, each being a continuous image of a separable metric space. Perhaps we can define a metric on K by combining metrics from each A_n, but we need to address whether those subspaces are closed. I might have to explore different methods to show K's properties clearly.

**Finding a countable base for K**

I'm exploring how to demonstrate that our compact Hausdorff space K has a countable base, which is crucial for its metrizability. Each A_n is metrizable and has a countable base, and since K is the union of these spaces, a natural approach would be to create a base for K from the union of the bases from each A_n. By checking that any open set in K intersects with these bases, I can confirm that we have a countable base for the entire space K. So, if every point in K can be surrounded by these base sets, we're set!

**Proving K's metrizability**

I'm establishing that K is separable and second countable to show it's metrizable. In a compact Hausdorff (CH) space, being second countable implies metrizability, supported by the Urysohn Metrization Theorem. I can demonstrate this by showing that the union of standard countable bases for each A_n forms a countable base for K. By picking appropriate open sets from K and combining bases from the A_n, I can confirm that K meets the criteria for metrizability efficiently. This seems to be the standard approach!

Solution Explanation:

Let K be a compact Hausdorff space which is written as an increasing union K = ⋃(n=0 to ∞) Aₙ of metrizable subspaces Aₙ ⊂ Aₘ for n < m. We claim that K is metrizable.

Step 1: Each Aₙ has a countable base.  
Because Aₙ is metrizable, it has a countable base βₙ for its subspace topology. Concretely, βₙ = {Uₙ,i : i ∈ ℕ}, and each Uₙ,i is open in Aₙ (in the subspace topology).

Step 2: Form a candidate base for K.  
Consider the family  
  β = ⋃(n=0 to ∞) βₙ.  
Although each βₙ is countable, β is still a countable union of countable sets, hence β is countable.

Step 3: β is indeed a basis for the topology on K.  
We must check that for every open set O ⊆ K and every point x ∈ O, there is some B ∈ β with x ∈ B ⊆ O.

• Since x ∈ O ⊆ K, pick any n so that x ∈ Aₙ (this is possible because K = ⋃ₙ Aₙ).  
• Now O ∩ Aₙ is an open neighborhood of x in the subspace topology of Aₙ.  
• Because βₙ is a base for Aₙ, there exists some B ∈ βₙ with x ∈ B ⊆ (O ∩ Aₙ).  
• But B ⊆ O ∩ Aₙ implies B ⊆ O. Thus we have found the required B ∈ β with x ∈ B ⊆ O.

Hence β is a base for the topology of K.

Step 4: Conclude that K is metrizable.  
Since β is countable, K is second-countable. A classical theorem (the Urysohn Metrization Theorem) states that any second-countable, Hausdorff, and regular (in fact normal) space is metrizable. Because K is compact Hausdorff (hence normal), we deduce K is metrizable.

Thus the increasing union of metrizable subspaces Aₙ covers all of K and forces K itself to have a countable base, completing the proof.

question: A liquid is moving in an infinite pipe. For each molecule if it is at point with coordinate  $x$  then after  $t$  seconds it will be at a point of  $p(t,x)$ . Prove that if  $p(t,x)$  is a polynomial of  $t,x$  then speed of all molecules are equal and constant.
response:
**Exploring fluid motion**

I'm diving into a fluid dynamics problem where a liquid moves through an infinite pipe, and we need to prove that if the position function p(t, x) is a polynomial in both t and x, then all molecules share the same constant speed. This is interesting because we'll show that velocity, defined as the partial derivative of p(t, x) with respect to t, remains constant. I should clarify that x represents the initial position of each fluid particle along its trajectory p(t, x) at time t.

**Analyzing molecular velocity**

I'm examining the velocity of a molecule that started at position x, defined as v(t, x) = ∂p(t, x)/∂t. I want to show that if p(t, x) is a polynomial in t and x, then all molecules share the same constant velocity that doesn’t depend on x. 

The polynomial form means p(t, x) can be expressed as a sum of terms involving coefficients and powers of t and x. By demonstrating that p satisfies a specific flow invariance condition, I can conclude that the velocity remains consistent across molecules for an incompressible fluid. I'm intrigued by the constraints this polynomial form imposes!

**Establishing polynomial solutions**

I'm analyzing the functional equation f(s+t) = f(s)f(t) without constraints, which typically has exponential solutions like f(x) = e^{cx} or f(x) = 0. But since we're looking for polynomial solutions, it limits f to being identically 0 or 1.

Considering the requirement that p(0, x) = x, I realize a_1(t) must equal 1. Then, the group property leads to a_0(t) having a linear form. This gives p(t, x) = x + ct, proving that velocity v(t, x) = c is constant for all molecules, confirming uniform speed across the fluid!

First, let us restate the problem in slightly more precise terms:

Problem Statement.  
Suppose we have a one-dimensional flow describing the motion of fluid particles in an infinite pipe.  Label a particle by its initial position x (at time t = 0).  After time t, the position of this same particle is p(t, x).  Assume p is a polynomial in the two variables t and x.  Show that p(t, x) must be of the form  
p(t, x) = x + c t  
for some constant c, and therefore all particles move with the same constant velocity.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. The Flow (or Semigroup) Property
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Because p(t, x) describes the motion of particles (the flow of fluid), it must satisfy the usual flow (or semigroup) property:

(1)   p(t₁ + t₂, x) = p(t₁, p(t₂, x)),       for all x and all t₁, t₂ ≥ 0.

This property encodes the idea that if you flow for time t₂ starting at x, and then flow for another time t₁ starting at the position p(t₂, x), it is the same as flowing for total time t₁ + t₂ starting at x.

We also have the initial condition

(2)   p(0, x) = x   for all x,

since each particle labeled by x starts at x when t = 0.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Polynomial Form of p
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

We assume p(t, x) is a polynomial in the variables (t, x).  Write it in the general form

p(t, x) = a₀(t) + a₁(t) x + a₂(t) x² + … + aₙ(t) xⁿ,

where each aᵢ(t) is itself a polynomial in t.  (Only finitely many terms appear.)

The conditions (1) and (2) will force severe restrictions on this polynomial expansion.  Below we show that all higher-order terms in x must vanish, and that p must reduce to an affine linear function in x of a specific simpler form.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Using the Flow (Semigroup) Property
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3.1. Evaluate both sides of (1).

Left side:  p(t₁ + t₂, x)  
     = a₀(t₁ + t₂) + a₁(t₁ + t₂) x + a₂(t₁ + t₂) x² + … + aₙ(t₁ + t₂) xⁿ.

Right side:  p(t₁, p(t₂, x))  
     = a₀(t₁) + a₁(t₁) [p(t₂, x)] + a₂(t₁) [p(t₂, x)]² + … + aₙ(t₁) [p(t₂, x)]ⁿ,

where

p(t₂, x) = a₀(t₂) + a₁(t₂) x + a₂(t₂) x² + … + aₙ(t₂) xⁿ.

Hence the right-hand side becomes a complicated polynomial in x, obtained by substituting the polynomial in x (that is p(t₂, x)) into another polynomial in the “variable” y = p(t₂, x).  

3.2. Matching both sides as polynomials in x.

Since these two polynomials in x must be identical for all x and all t₁, t₂, every coefficient of x^k must match.  One can check that unless all but one of the aᵢ(t) vanish, the structure of substituting polynomials into polynomials will produce higher-degree terms that cannot match a simple polynomial of the same total degree in x.  

A more straightforward way to see this is: the only way p(t₁ + t₂, x) and p(t₁, p(t₂, x)) can match as polynomials in x for all t₁, t₂ is if p is at most linear in x:

p(t, x) = a₀(t) + a₁(t) x.

Indeed, if there were any terms a₂(t) x² + … + aₙ(t) xⁿ with n ≥ 2, the substitution on the right side would introduce (p(t₂, x))², etc., which generally produces powers of x up to x^(2n), contradicting the assumption that the total must match as a single polynomial up to x^n.  

Hence,

p(t, x) = a₀(t) + a₁(t) x

is forced by the flow property plus the requirement of being polynomial in t and x.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Determining a₀(t) and a₁(t)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

4.1. Check the initial condition p(0, x) = x.

Putting t = 0 in p(t, x) = a₀(t) + a₁(t) x gives  
p(0, x) = a₀(0) + a₁(0) x.

But we need p(0, x) = x for all x.  Thus  
a₀(0) = 0, and  a₁(0) = 1.

4.2. Enforce the semigroup equation again.

From (1), we have:

p(t₁ + t₂, x) = p(t₁, p(t₂, x)),

i.e.

a₀(t₁ + t₂) + a₁(t₁ + t₂) x  
= a₀(t₁) + a₁(t₁) [a₀(t₂) + a₁(t₂) x].

Matching constant and x-coefficients separately, we get two independent functional equations:

• For the constant term:  
  a₀(t₁ + t₂) = a₀(t₁) + a₁(t₁) a₀(t₂).  

• For the x-coefficient:  
  a₁(t₁ + t₂) = a₁(t₁) a₁(t₂).

4.3. Solve for a₁(t).

The equation

a₁(t₁ + t₂) = a₁(t₁) a₁(t₂)

is the standard functional equation for exponentials.  Under the requirement that a₁(t) be a polynomial in t, the only solutions are the constant polynomial solutions a₁(t) ≡ 0 or a₁(t) ≡ 1, or else a₁(t) = cᵗ for c ∈ ℝ.  But cᵗ is not a polynomial in t unless c = 0 or c = 1.  

Since a₁(0) = 1, we must choose c = 1; hence a₁(t) ≡ 1.

4.4. Solve for a₀(t).

Now that a₁(t) ≡ 1, the functional equation for a₀ becomes

a₀(t₁ + t₂) = a₀(t₁) + a₀(t₂).

Again, insisting that a₀(t) be a polynomial in t forces the classical solution of the “Cauchy functional equation” in polynomials:

a₀(t) = c t,

for some constant c.  (If one allowed more general functions, one could have more exotic solutions, but under continuity—and in particular, under the requirement that it be a polynomial—this is forced to be linear.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Conclusion: Constant Velocity
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Putting it all together,

p(t, x) = a₀(t) + a₁(t) x = c t + x,

with c constant and a₁(t) ≡ 1.

Hence, the velocity of the fluid particle initially at x is

v(t, x) = ∂/∂t [p(t, x)] = c,

which is independent of t and x.  Consequently, all particles move with the same constant speed c, and we have shown what was required:

If p(t, x) is a polynomial in t and x and satisfies the flow property, then p(t,x) must be x + c t for some constant c, and therefore all fluid molecules move with the same constant velocity.

question:
The reaction of silver and oxygen to silver oxide Ag2O has a standard Gibbs free energy (deltaG) of -22 kJ/mol (25 centigrade, 101300 Pa). What is the partial pressure of oxygen gas in the vessel under the mentioned standard conditions? (Consider the gases as ideal gases.)
